questions.body: Which runtime data area in the JVM is shared across all executing threads?
questions.keyPoints: The Heap and Metaspace (method area) are shared by all threads; Program Counter, JVM Stack, and Native Method Stack are per-thread.

options.text: Heap Memory and Metaspace (Method Area)
options.explanation: Heap (storing object instances) and Metaspace (storing class metadata, static fields) are created on JVM startup and shared across all threads. Stacks and PC registers are allocated per thread.

options.text: The JVM Stack and Program Counter (PC) Register
options.explanation: Each thread has its own private JVM stack and Program Counter register.

options.text: Native Method Stack only
options.explanation: Native method stacks are allocated per-thread for native C/C++ method invocations.

options.text: Thread Local Storage (TLS) buffers
options.explanation: Thread-local storage is private to each respective thread.

questions.body: In Java, what happens to local primitive variables declared inside a method when the method finishes execution and returns?
questions.keyPoints: Local variables on the call stack frame are popped and deallocated immediately upon method return without GC involvement.

options.text: Their stack frame is popped from the JVM call stack, automatically freeing their memory immediately without GC involvement.
options.explanation: Stack memory allocation is LIFO. When a method returns, its entire stack frame (holding local primitives and references) is popped immediately.

options.text: They are placed in the Young Generation Eden space awaiting Minor GC.
options.explanation: Stack primitives do not live on the heap and are never collected by GC.

options.text: They are moved to Metaspace as permanent class definitions.
options.explanation: Metaspace holds class metadata, not local method variables.

options.text: They persist until the operating system terminates the JVM process.
options.explanation: Stack frames exist only for the duration of the method invocation.

questions.body: Starting in Java 8, what major architectural change replaced the old Permanent Generation (PermGen)?
questions.keyPoints: PermGen was replaced by Metaspace, which uses native off-heap memory instead of JVM heap.

options.text: PermGen was replaced by Metaspace, which stores class metadata in OS native off-heap memory rather than contiguous JVM heap.
options.explanation: PermGen had a fixed contiguous heap size prone to java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space. Metaspace uses native memory, resizing dynamically up to available OS memory (or -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize).

options.text: PermGen was converted into a Redis-backed distributed cache.
options.explanation: Metaspace is native process memory inside the local JVM, not an external network cache.

options.text: PermGen was moved to the Young Generation Survivor spaces.
options.explanation: Survivor spaces are part of the heap for short-lived young objects.

options.text: PermGen was eliminated by removing all runtime class metadata entirely.
options.explanation: Class metadata is essential for reflection and dynamic dispatch; it was simply moved to native Metaspace.

questions.body: What is the 'Weak Generational Hypothesis' that justifies splitting JVM heap into Young and Old generations?
questions.keyPoints: The weak generational hypothesis observes that most objects die shortly after creation, and objects surviving several GC cycles tend to live for a long time.

options.text: Most allocated objects die shortly after creation (have very short lifespans), while objects that survive several GC cycles tend to live for a long time.
options.explanation: Empirical data shows >95% of objects die young. Generational collectors optimize for this by focusing frequent Minor GCs on a small Eden space where reclaiming dead objects is fast.

options.text: Objects created by background threads are weaker and collectable faster than main-thread objects.
options.explanation: Thread ownership does not dictate generational categorization.

options.text: Static variables always leak memory unless explicitly assigned to null.
options.explanation: Static variables are referenced by Class objects in Metaspace/heap, not the generational hypothesis.

options.text: Garbage collection algorithms degrade in performance as CPU core count increases.
options.explanation: Modern GC algorithms (G1, ZGC) scale with multi-core CPUs.

questions.body: During a Minor GC in the Young Generation, what is the role of the two Survivor spaces (S0 / From and S1 / To)?
questions.keyPoints: Copying collector copies live objects from Eden and the From survivor space to the To survivor space, alternating roles.

options.text: Live objects from Eden and the 'From' survivor space are copied into the 'To' survivor space; the roles of S0 and S1 then alternate, preventing heap fragmentation.
options.explanation: The Young Gen uses a copying collector. Live objects survive into one Survivor space while the other remains empty. With each cycle, surviving objects increment an age counter until tenured.

options.text: S0 stores primitive data types while S1 stores reference pointers.
options.explanation: Both survivor spaces hold full Java objects.

options.text: S0 is read-only while S1 is write-only.
options.explanation: They alternate roles with each Minor GC cycle.

options.text: Objects in S0 are compressed using GZIP before writing to S1.
options.explanation: Survivor spaces do not compress objects using GZIP.

questions.body: When does an object in the Young Generation get promoted ('tenured') to the Old (Tenured) Generation?
questions.keyPoints: An object is promoted when its age exceeds MaxTenuringThreshold or when Survivor space becomes full (premature promotion).

options.text: When its survival count exceeds the -XX:MaxTenuringThreshold or when dynamic tenuring threshold rules trigger due to survivor space overflow.
options.explanation: Objects that survive enough Minor GC cycles reach the tenuring threshold (default up to 15) and get moved to Old Gen. High allocation rates can trigger premature promotion.

options.text: Whenever an object's size exceeds 64 bytes.
options.explanation: Size alone does not trigger promotion, though very large arrays can be directly allocated in Old Gen via PretenureSizeThreshold.

options.text: When the object is serialized to disk or sent over a socket.
options.explanation: I/O serialization has no bearing on GC generation placement.

options.text: When the thread that allocated the object terminates.
options.explanation: Object lifespan depends on reachability from GC roots, not allocating thread termination.

questions.body: Which of the following qualifies as a 'GC Root' during the reachability analysis phase of garbage collection?
questions.keyPoints: GC roots include local variables on thread stacks, active threads, static class fields, and JNI global references.

options.text: Local variables on active thread call stacks, static fields of loaded classes, and JNI handles.
options.explanation: GC roots are objects directly accessible outside the heap: active thread stacks, JNI references, static variables referenced by Class objects, and system classes.

options.text: Any object that has been allocated for more than 10 minutes.
options.explanation: Object age does not make it a GC root; unreferenced old objects are garbage.

options.text: Null pointer references stored in local arrays.
options.explanation: Null references point to nothing and cannot anchor an object graph.

options.text: Any object whose hashCode() returns an even integer.
options.explanation: Hash codes are unrelated to GC reachability.

questions.body: What does a 'Stop-the-World' (STW) pause mean in the context of Java Garbage Collection?
questions.keyPoints: STW pauses suspend all application mutator threads at safe points so the GC can inspect or move objects safely.

options.text: All application mutator threads are brought to safe points and halted while the garbage collector performs critical heap inspections or object movements.
options.explanation: During STW, application threads pause at bytecode safe points, preventing state mutations while GC threads scan roots, remap references, or compact memory.

options.text: The entire operating system freezes all processes including kernel background daemons.
options.explanation: STW only pauses the threads of the specific JVM instance.

options.text: Network interfaces discard all incoming TCP packets permanently.
options.explanation: TCP packets buffer in OS socket buffers while the JVM is paused.

options.text: The JVM crashes and writes a core dump to disk.
options.explanation: STW is normal expected GC behavior, not a JVM crash.

questions.body: How does the Garbage-First (G1) collector divide the JVM heap compared to traditional collectors like ParallelGC?
questions.keyPoints: G1 partitions the heap into equal-sized virtual regions (1MB to 32MB) assigned roles dynamically, rather than contiguous fixed generational spaces.

options.text: It divides the heap into thousands of equal-sized independent regions (1MB–32MB) dynamically assigned as Eden, Survivor, Old, or Humongous.
options.explanation: G1 replaces contiguous generation boundaries with non-contiguous regional blocks. It tracks garbage density per region and prioritizes collecting regions with the most garbage ('Garbage-First').

options.text: It allocates a separate physical RAM stick for each individual Java thread.
options.explanation: G1 manages standard virtual memory allocated to the JVM heap.

options.text: It restricts the total heap size to a maximum of 2GB.
options.explanation: G1 is designed specifically for large multi-gigabyte heaps (>4GB up to hundreds of GBs).

options.text: It eliminates the Old Generation completely and retains only Eden.
options.explanation: G1 retains generational concepts; regions are dynamically assigned generational roles.

questions.body: How does ZGC achieve sub-millisecond maximum pause times even on multi-terabyte heaps?
questions.keyPoints: ZGC performs marking, relocation, and reference updating concurrently with application threads using colored pointers and load barriers.

options.text: It performs all heavy GC phases (marking, relocation, and reference remapping) concurrently with application threads using colored pointers and load barriers.
options.explanation: ZGC uses 64-bit colored pointers (encoding metadata in reference address bits) and JIT-compiled load barriers. If an application thread accesses an object mid-relocation, the load barrier repairs the reference on the fly.

options.text: It never frees memory and relies on infinite cloud virtual memory paging.
options.explanation: ZGC actively compacts and reclaims physical heap pages.

options.text: It runs exclusively on single-threaded ARM microcontrollers.
options.explanation: ZGC is a scalable enterprise collector for x86_64 and AArch64 multi-core servers.

options.text: It turns off type checking and bytecode verification in the class loader.
options.explanation: Class loading and bytecode verification are unaffected by ZGC.

questions.body: When does the Garbage Collector reclaim an object that is ONLY weakly reachable via a `java.lang.ref.WeakReference`?
questions.keyPoints: Weakly reachable objects are collected during the very next garbage collection cycle regardless of available heap memory.

options.text: During the very next garbage collection cycle, regardless of whether memory is constrained or plentiful.
options.explanation: WeakReference objects are cleared eagerly upon the next GC when no strong references remain. SoftReferences, by contrast, are retained until memory pressure requires reclamation.

options.text: Only when the JVM is about to throw an OutOfMemoryError.
options.explanation: SoftReference objects are cleared under memory pressure before OOM; WeakReferences are cleared immediately on next GC.

options.text: Only when the developer calls System.gc() explicitly.
options.explanation: GC cycles run autonomously without requiring explicit System.gc() calls.

options.text: Never; weak references prevent garbage collection indefinitely.
options.explanation: Strong references prevent collection; weak references do not.

questions.body: What is the primary use case of `PhantomReference` and `java.lang.ref.Cleaner` over the deprecated `finalize()` method?
questions.keyPoints: PhantomReference and Cleaner allow safe off-heap resource cleanup without resurrection risks or unpredictability associated with finalize().

options.text: Reliable pre-mortem cleanup of off-heap/native resources without object resurrection risks or unpredictable finalizer thread blocking.
options.explanation: finalize() had severe flaws: unpredictable execution timing, thread starvation, and zombie object resurrection. PhantomReference/Cleaner provide safe, explicit notification when an object is phantom reachable.

options.text: Accelerating JSON parsing through CPU SIMD instructions.
options.explanation: Reference queues deal with lifecycle cleanup, not JSON parsing.

options.text: Automatically restarting terminated thread pools.
options.explanation: Cleaners do not manage thread pool lifecycle.

options.text: Ensuring database transactions are automatically committed upon garbage collection.
options.explanation: Database transactions must be explicitly committed or rolled back via JDBC/connection managers.

questions.body: Which scenario is the most frequent root cause of `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` in production Spring Boot microservices?
questions.keyPoints: Unbounded caches, unpaged database queries loading millions of rows, or memory leaks where static or long-lived collections retain references.

options.text: Unbounded in-memory collections (e.g. static maps without eviction) or unpaged database queries loading millions of entities into memory.
options.explanation: When objects remain reachable through live root references (like static caches, unpaginated SELECT * lists, or thread locals), GC cannot reclaim them, exhausting available heap space.

options.text: Exceeding the maximum recursive method call stack depth.
options.explanation: Exceeding call stack depth throws java.lang.StackOverflowError, not heap OutOfMemoryError.

options.text: Calling Math.random() too many times within a single loop.
options.explanation: Primitive math operations allocate zero heap memory.

options.text: Creating more than 10 classes in the same package.
options.explanation: Class definitions consume small Metaspace memory, not gigabytes of heap.

questions.body: What optimization does the JVM JIT compiler perform via Escape Analysis when an object does not escape the allocating method scope?
questions.keyPoints: Scalar replacement: the compiler avoids heap allocation and breaks the object into individual primitive fields stored in CPU registers or stack.

options.text: Scalar Replacement: the object is decomposed into its constituent primitive fields, allocated directly on the stack or in CPU registers, eliminating heap allocation.
options.explanation: If Escape Analysis proves an object reference never leaves the method (does not escape), JIT avoids heap allocation and GC overhead by decomposing it into scalar variables (scalar replacement) or allocating it on the stack.

options.text: It serializes the object to temporary disk swap space.
options.explanation: Disk serialization would be orders of magnitude slower than heap allocation.

options.text: It promotes the object immediately to the Old Generation Tenured space.
options.explanation: Non-escaping objects should die with the method, not be tenured to Old Gen.

options.text: It encrypts the object references to protect against reflection attacks.
options.explanation: Escape analysis is purely a JIT performance optimization.

questions.body: In the HotSpot JVM's Tiered Compilation model, what are the distinct roles of the C1 (Client) and C2 (Server) compilers?
questions.keyPoints: Tier 1-3 (C1) compiles quickly with lightweight profiling for fast startup; Tier 4 (C2) applies aggressive speculative optimizations for peak throughput.

options.text: C1 compiles code quickly with lightweight profiling to achieve rapid startup; C2 optimizes hot code paths aggressively using profiling data to maximize peak throughput.
options.explanation: Tiered compilation combines fast startup (Tier 1-3 / C1 compiler with basic inlining and checks) with maximum peak steady-state performance (Tier 4 / C2 compiler with loop unrolling, escape analysis, and inlining).

options.text: C1 compiles Java code to JavaScript while C2 compiles Java code to WebAssembly.
options.explanation: Both C1 and C2 compile Java bytecode to native machine instructions for the host CPU architecture.

options.text: C1 runs only on 32-bit CPUs, while C2 runs only on 64-bit CPUs.
options.explanation: Tiered compilation runs both C1 and C2 dynamically on standard 64-bit systems.

options.text: C1 handles class loading while C2 handles thread context switching.
options.explanation: Both are JIT compilation stages converting hot bytecode to native machine instructions.

questions.body: What is the standard parent-delegation model used by Java ClassLoaders when loading a class?
questions.keyPoints: A classloader delegates loading to its parent first; only if the parent fails (ClassNotFoundException) does the child attempt to load it.

options.text: A classloader first delegates the load request to its parent classloader; only if parent fails (ClassNotFoundException) does the child attempt to find and load the class.
options.explanation: Parent-delegation ensures fundamental core classes (like java.lang.Object) are always loaded by the Bootstrap ClassLoader, preventing malicious substitution of trusted classes.

options.text: Child classloaders always load classes first to allow overriding standard JDK system classes.
options.explanation: Child-first loading violates standard delegation (used selectively only in web servlet containers for WEB-INF/classes).

options.text: All classloaders simultaneously query Maven Central over HTTPS.
options.explanation: Classloaders read from local classpath and filesystem jars, not Maven Central at runtime.

options.text: Classes are loaded randomly across available CPU cores without hierarchy.
options.explanation: Class loading follows a strict hierarchical delegation chain.

questions.body: What does the JVM flag `-XX:+UseCompressedOops` do, and what is the maximum heap size where it remains effective?
questions.keyPoints: UseCompressedOops compresses 64-bit object reference pointers into 32 bits by using 8-byte alignment, effective up to 32 GB heap size.

options.text: It encodes 64-bit object references as 32-bit relative pointers by shifting by 3 bits (8-byte object alignment), effective on heaps up to ~32GB.
options.explanation: Since all Java heap objects are 8-byte aligned, the lowest 3 bits are always 0. Shifting references enables 32-bit integers to address up to 2^35 bytes (32 GB) of heap, saving 50% pointer cache space.

options.text: It compresses String values using LZ4 compression algorithm.
options.explanation: String compression is handled by Compact Strings (-XX:+CompactStrings), not Compressed OOPs.

options.text: It limits the maximum number of methods in any single Java class to 65,536.
options.explanation: That is the JVM constant pool index limit (0xFFFF), not compressed oops.

options.text: It restricts the JVM to only run on 32-bit hardware architectures.
options.explanation: Compressed OOPs specifically optimize 64-bit JVMs on heaps below 32 GB.

questions.body: When troubleshooting a 100% CPU spike in a production Java process, how do you map a high-CPU thread ID from Linux `top -H -p <pid>` to a Java thread dump?
questions.keyPoints: Convert the Linux thread LWP decimal ID to hexadecimal and look for the matching 'nid=0x...' in the jstack/thread dump.

options.text: Convert the Linux thread ID (LWP) from decimal to hexadecimal and search for the matching native thread identifier (nid=0x...) in the jstack thread dump.
options.explanation: In HotSpot thread dumps, each thread entry shows 'nid=0x<hex>'. Converting the Linux thread PID (LWP) to hex (e.g. 12345 -> 0x3039) immediately identifies the exact thread stack causing CPU burn.

options.text: Multiply the process ID by the number of CPU cores and check the JVM log file.
options.explanation: Process ID multiplication has no meaning in thread mapping.

options.text: Recompile the application with debugging symbols and inspect the heap dump with Wireshark.
options.explanation: Wireshark is a packet capture tool, not a thread analyzer.

options.text: Linux thread IDs cannot be mapped to Java threads because of JVM bytecode abstraction.
options.explanation: HotSpot maps Java platform threads 1:1 to OS kernel threads and includes their native ID (nid) in thread dumps.

questions.body: In memory profilers like Eclipse Memory Analyzer (MAT), what is the difference between 'Shallow Size' and 'Retained Size' of an object?
questions.keyPoints: Shallow size is the memory consumed by the object itself; Retained size is the memory that would be freed if this object was garbage collected.

options.text: Shallow size is the memory consumed by the object's own fields; Retained size is total memory freed if this object is GC'd (shallow size + exclusively reachable referenced objects).
options.explanation: Shallow size accounts only for the instance structure and pointer references. Retained size represents the dominator tree footprint: memory that would be reclaimed if the object was collected.

options.text: Shallow size applies to Young Gen, while Retained size applies to Old Gen.
options.explanation: Shallow and retained sizes are mathematical graph concepts applicable to any object.

options.text: Shallow size includes all circular references, while Retained size excludes them.
options.explanation: Retained size calculates dominator reachability, handling cycles accurately.

options.text: Shallow size is stored in CPU cache, while Retained size resides on the SSD swap file.
options.explanation: Both metrics measure heap RAM allocation.

questions.body: Why do high-performance networking frameworks like Netty use Direct ByteBuffers (`ByteBuffer.allocateDirect()`) instead of Heap ByteBuffers?
questions.keyPoints: Direct ByteBuffers use native off-heap memory, enabling zero-copy OS socket I/O without copying data through intermediate JVM heap buffers.

options.text: They allocate memory off-heap, allowing native OS socket I/O system calls to read/write directly without copying bytes through intermediate JVM heap buffers (Zero-Copy I/O).
options.explanation: For heap buffers, the OS cannot safely access memory during I/O because GC might move objects mid-transfer; the JVM must copy to a temporary direct buffer first. Direct ByteBuffers bypass this copy.

options.text: Direct ByteBuffers are immune to buffer overflow attacks.
options.explanation: Buffer limits are checked by the ByteBuffer class, but they are not an encryption or anti-exploit system.

options.text: Direct ByteBuffers are automatically compressed using Brotli compression.
options.explanation: Direct ByteBuffers store raw uncompressed bytes.

options.text: Direct ByteBuffers bypass TCP handshake requirements for faster connections.
options.explanation: TCP handshakes are handled by the OS kernel network stack.
